justification: Technical round 1 for /csharp-dotnet/linq-deferred-execution/. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/linq-deferred-execution.md` from PowerShell: PASS, blocks=22, executed=11, run three consecutive times with identical output every time (no flakiness, including the 200,000-element prime-sieve timing block, which is wildcarded for ms but exact for the prime counts and the SLA/lookup call counts, which are exact and reproduced all three runs). I traced the double-enumeration bug by hand against the printed output: `urgent.Count()` walks the Where iterator once (4 predicate calls on 4 tickets), the following `foreach` re-enumerates the same deferred query from the start (4 more calls) = 8, matching 'SLA service calls: 8' exactly; the second exercise (Any/foreach/Count = 2+3+3 = 8) checks out the same way. Both are genuine, not asserted. The mine-vs-real trace comparison (id=compare) is real, not cosmetic: swapping MyWhere/MySelect for Where/Select and relabelling produces line-for-line identical interleaving (source-yield -> test -> project, one element deep before the next is pulled), which is the correct behavioral signature of a pull-based iterator pipeline and is exactly what the classification table calls 'streaming.' The IQueryable proof is genuinely sound: `query.Expression` is inspected via casts to MethodCallExpression -> (Quote-)LambdaExpression -> BinaryExpression -> MemberExpression/ConstantExpression, and `property.Member.Name` / `target.Value` read reflection metadata and a boxed constant directly off the tree. Nothing in the inspect block calls `.Compile()`, invokes the lambda, or otherwise executes it; `Console.WriteLine($'{call.Arguments[1]}')` in the block before it only calls `Expression.ToString()`, which is a textual tree-walk, not execution. I independently confirmed against the dotnet/runtime source that `Queryable.Where` really does build `Expression.Call(..., source.Expression, Expression.Quote(predicate))`, which is exactly the Quote-wrapped shape the article's `Unquote` helper handles - this is not a simplified toy model, it is what the real Where overload does. All 7 cited sources are real and I fetched all of them; every direct quotation in the article is verbatim: 'Calling an iterator doesn't execute it immediately' (yield statement page, correctly attributed there and not to the Iterators page), 'is supported directly in the C# language by the yield keyword' (Deferred execution and lazy evaluation), 'at the point in the code where the query is declared' / 'when the query variable is enumerated' / 'the results might differ every time' (Introduction to LINQ Queries), 'stores all the information that is required to perform the action' / 'not executed until the object is enumerated' (Enumerable.Where remarks), 'causes the expression tree ... to be executed' / 'the definition of executing an expression tree is specific to a query provider' / 'may involve translating the expression tree to an appropriate query language' (IQueryable remarks), and 'generates a MethodCallExpression' (Queryable.Where remarks, paraphrased accurately as 'hands it to the source's IQueryProvider,' which matches the page's CreateQuery(Expression) description). The deferred/immediate/streaming/nonstreaming classification is verified against the live 'Introduction to LINQ Queries' page, which today contains an H2 section literally titled 'Classification of standard query operators by manner of execution' with the full operator table (Where/Select streaming, OrderBy/GroupBy nonstreaming, Count/ToList/First immediate all confirmed against the live table) - the content the writer says used to live on its own dedicated page really has been folded in here, and the separate legacy URL (.../linq/classification-of-standard-query-operators-by-manner-of-execution) really does 404 when fetched directly, so this is a verified fact, not an invented redirect story. EnumerableQuery<T> checks out too: its own docs describe it as rewriting the expression tree to call Enumerable methods and executing it against the underlying IEnumerable<T>, i.e. in-process, not against a remote provider, matching the article's description. The re-enumeration cost measurement is a fair comparison: `expensive` is genuinely re-evaluated from `Enumerable.Range` through `Where` on both `.Count()` calls (both are deferred/streaming, so nothing is cached between them), and only `.ToList()` produces a real materialized `List<int>` whose `.Count` is an O(1) field read - the three-way comparison isolates exactly the variable the section is about. Comparing against Microsoft's own docs (purely descriptive, no code the reader runs, no rebuilt operators) and Jon Skeet's Edulinq series (the closest real precedent for 'rebuild LINQ from scratch to teach it,' but a 45-part book-length project, not a single page, and without this article's specific move of pairing a rebuilt pipeline against the real one in one side-by-side trace, or combining that with a runnable proof that IQueryable inspection never touches the predicate), this article's compression of bug -> mechanism -> rebuild-and-compare -> cost -> IQueryable proof into one coherent, fully-verified page is a genuine differentiator, not a rehash. Two issues keep it out of 8.5+ range. First, and most serious: the sentence 'The real Enumerable.Where and Enumerable.Select ... are, at heart, the same foreach loop with a yield return guarded by an if' is factually wrong about the current implementation. I pulled the actual dotnet/runtime source for Where.cs and Select.cs (linked from the article's own Enumerable.Where citation): the production Where and Select overloads used here (list/array/enumerable sources) are hand-written sealed iterator classes with an explicit `MoveNext()` state machine - there is no `yield return` anywhere in Where.cs, and Select.cs uses `yield return` only in the separate indexed-selector overload the article doesn't use. The compiler abandoned yield-return iterators for these hot paths specifically so it could add the IPartition/ICollection/array-length fast paths the article does correctly mention existing - but then asserts they are still 'at heart' compiler-generated iterators, which they no longer are. The behavioral claim the article actually proves (identical streaming order) survives this error untouched, since that's an empirical trace match, not a source-code claim, but the explanatory sentence is a specific, checkable, and wrong statement about how .NET is implemented, which is exactly the kind of error the rubric caps at 7. Second, more minor: the EnumerableQuery<T> paragraph (in-process provider, compiles the tree back into a delegate) is a non-obvious factual claim with no citation and the type isn't in the source list at all, even though a docs page for it exists and would have supported it - this is a sourcing gap under EDITORIAL_BRIEF.md rule 3, not a wrong claim (I verified it's correct). Smaller nit: the streaming definition ('reads source elements one at a time and can yield a result element after reading just one') slightly undersells Microsoft's own wording, which allows a streaming operator to read more than one source element before producing one result (e.g. SkipWhile/Distinct); true for Where/Select as used here, imprecise as a general definition.

issues.location: Writing `Where` and `Select` from scratch, closing paragraph after the id=compare code/output block: "The real Enumerable.Where and Enumerable.Select are more careful about edge cases ... but they are, at heart, the same foreach loop with a yield return guarded by an if."
issues.problem: This is factually wrong about the current CoreCLR implementation. Enumerable.Where and the non-indexed Enumerable.Select overloads (the ones exercised in this article) are hand-written sealed classes (e.g. ArrayWhereIterator<T>, IEnumerableWhereIterator<T>, ListSelectIterator<T,TResult>) that implement IEnumerator<T> manually via an explicit MoveNext() state machine. They do not use the `yield return` keyword at all; the compiler abandoned compiler-generated iterators here specifically to enable the ICollection/IPartition/array/list fast paths the article itself mentions in the same sentence. (Select.cs does use yield return, but only in the separate indexed-selector overload that this article never calls.) The article's own cited source for Enumerable.Where links directly to this Where.cs file.
issues.fixLooksLike: Change the closing sentence to something like: 'The real Enumerable.Where and Enumerable.Select behave the same way - pull one element at a time, test or project it, yield or move on - but for performance they are not literally written with yield return: modern .NET implements them as hand-written MoveNext() state machines with extra fast paths for arrays, lists and known-length sources, rather than compiler-generated iterators.' This keeps the (correct, proven) behavioral claim and drops the (wrong) implementation claim.

issues.location: Deferred, immediate, streaming, nonstreaming, bullet definition of Streaming: "reads source elements one at a time and can yield a result element after reading just one"
issues.problem: Slightly undersells Microsoft's own definition, which explicitly allows a streaming operator to read more than one source element before it can yield a result ('A streaming operator continues to read source elements until a result element can be produced. This means that more than one source element might be read to produce one result element.') - true of SkipWhile, Distinct, etc. The article's phrasing is accurate for Where/Select specifically (which is all it's illustrating) but reads as the general definition.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either scope the sentence explicitly to Where/Select ('for an element-at-a-time test like Where's, it can yield after reading just one') or add the 'may need more than one' caveat Microsoft's definition carries.
